Cantilever mechanics and feedback control

Why the tiny diving board at the heart of an AFM behaves the way it does, and what limits how fast the machine can film molecules. A summary of Chapters 2 and 3 of a book on high-speed AFM (HS-AFM), written for graduate students in biology.

The two ideas to take away. (1) The cantilever is a spring whose stiffness and speed are set by its size. Short, thin levers are soft and fast. (2) AFM imaging is a chase: the scanner follows the surface with a delay, and that delay limits both imaging speed and how gently the tip can treat a fragile sample.

Chapter 2

Cantilever mechanics

Everything in AFM relies on a cantilever beam as the sensor, so this chapter works out how a uniform beam of length L, width w and thickness d bends and vibrates. Think of a diving board fixed at one end.

2.1 Static mechanics: how the beam bends

When a force P pushes on the beam, the upper surface stretches and the lower surface is compressed. The resistance to this bending depends on the material's Young's modulus E and on the cross-section through the area moment of inertia I = wd³/12.

For a force at the free end, the tip deflection is z0 = −PL³/(3EI), which gives the spring constant of the cantilever:

kc = 3EI / L³ = E w d³ / (4 L³)

Stiffness rises with the cube of thickness and falls with the cube of length. So thin, short levers can still be very soft. The energy stored in the bent beam is the familiar spring energy, Es = ½ kc z0².

The force is not always applied at the end. When the cantilever is excited acoustically by a piezo, a force acts uniformly along the whole beam. For the same tip displacement the total force then equals (8/3) kc z0 and the stored energy is (8/15) kc z0², about 7% more than for an end load. The simple spring picture is useful, but it is only exact for an end load.

2.2 Dynamic mechanics: how the beam vibrates

Solving the equation of motion with no external force gives a series of vibration modes (eigenmodes). The allowed shapes are described by numbers βn = 1.875, 4.694, 7.855, 10.996, 14.137 … for n = 1, 2, 3 …, and the resonant frequencies are:

ωn = βn² · (d / L²) · √(E / 12ρ)

Here ρ is the material density. The resonance rises with thickness and falls with the square of length, so short, thin cantilevers resonate at high frequency, which is exactly what fast imaging needs. Higher modes have frequencies of 6.27, 17.55, 34.39 and 56.85 times the first, and the beam takes the shapes in Fig. 2.2.

  • First mode as a mass on a spring. It behaves like a massless spring kc with an effective mass of 3/β1⁴ × m ≈ 0.24 m, where m is the actual mass of the beam. Then ω1 = √(kc / 0.24 m).
  • Higher modes are much stiffer. For a given tip deflection the kinetic energy grows with ωn², so the effective spring constant grows as βn⁴, about 39 times larger for n = 2. Higher modes are therefore generally not suitable for fragile biological samples.
  • Rayleigh method. For oscillation that is not free, the exact equation is hard to solve. Equating the maximum kinetic energy with the maximum strain energy gives ω1 = √(4.15 kc / m), i.e. the same effective mass 0.24 m.
Chapter 3

Feedback control and imaging rate

To keep the tip–sample force constant, the scanner has to respond to the surface in real time. It cannot, because every part of the feedback loop takes time to respond. Faster imaging means shorter delays.

The feedback loop and its delays

Delays of the individual components add up as the signal goes around the loop. The mechanical parts (cantilever and scanner) are generally slower than the electronics. Chapter 4 of the book covers how to optimise each one.

ComponentDelayNotes
Cantilever responseτc = Qc / (π fc)fc is the first resonant frequency in water
Parachuting timeτpIncluded in the PID response time
Deflection-to-amplitude conversionτda = 1 / (n fc)n (≥ 1) depends on the conversion method
PID controllerτPID ∝ (h0/A0) sin(θ/2) / fch0 sample height, A0 free amplitude, θ phase delay (π/4 at fB)
Z-scannerτz = θz / (2π fd) or Qz / (π fz)Depends on how the scanner is driven
Other electronicsδPiezo driver, photodiode sensor, etc.

3.1 The highest possible imaging rate

The speed of the feedback is summarised by the feedback bandwidth fB: the frequency at which the Z-scanner lags the sample height by a phase of π/4. From the total open-loop delay, fB ≈ 1/(8τopen). For example, fB = 50 kHz needs τopen of roughly 2.5 µs.

To see what that means for imaging, the chapter models the surface as a sine wave with period λ and height h0. When the stage scans at velocity Vx, the tip meets the bumps at frequency f = Vx/λ. The scanner follows with a phase delay θ, so the tip always sees a residual height error (blue line in Fig. 3.3).

That error means too much force on the uphill side and too little on the downhill side. Because fragile samples cannot tolerate this, the allowed phase delay θm must stay below π/4, and the scan velocity is limited to Vxmax = 4λfBθm/π. The raster scan covers each line twice (trace and retrace), which gives the maximum imaging rate:

Rmax = 2 λ fB θm / (π Ns Wx)

Rmax thus depends on the feedback bandwidth, the number of scan lines Ns, the scan range Wx and the sample fragility θm. It also depends on h0/A0, because that ratio affects fB.

Real samples are not sine waves

Real topography contains many spatial frequencies. Step edges aligned with the Y-direction contain high frequencies along X (Fig. 3.2), so the feedback error is large there. At rising steps the tip hits the sample hard, and at falling steps it loses contact.

The strategies used to reduce this disturbance:

  • Filaments: image those lying along the X-direction, as done for actin, to minimise step heights.
  • Globular proteins: raise their surface density to narrow the gaps between them (as for GroEL).
  • Small scan size: lowers the X velocity and keeps the frame rate high (as for F1-ATPase).
  • New X-scanning method (Chapter 8) and the dynamic PID controller (below).

Other limits also apply. In AC mode the tip must touch each pixel at least once per frame, so Rmax < fc/(2Np) (Np is the number of pixels). The X-scanner's top frequency gives Rmax < fxmax/Ns. In order of severity the restrictions are fB, then fc, then fxmax.

3.2 PID control and the parachuting problem

The Z-scanner is steered by a PID controller, which is easy to build in fast analog electronics or an FPGA. It receives the feedback error e(t) = A(t) − As (measured amplitude minus set point) and outputs:

O(t) = KP e(t) + KI ∫ e dt + KD de/dt
  • I (integral) responds to the past. It is slow but holds the scanner position once the error is zero, so it does most of the work.
  • P (proportional) responds to the present. It is quick but cannot hold a position alone.
  • D (derivative) anticipates the future. It damps oscillation but plays only a supporting role.

Raising the gains speeds up the response, but if the controller reacts faster than the loop delay it overshoots and rings, so the gains must be tuned. Even then a residual error always remains.

Parachuting. Let r = As/A0 be the set point relative to the free amplitude. If the tip's height D(t) drops below zero on a downhill region, the tip completely loses contact. In water the attraction is negligible, so nothing pulls it back. During this "parachuting" the error signal saturates at a small value, A0(1 − r), and the tip takes a long time to land again. In images it appears as bright lines along X with no topography (Fig. 3.4c).

Parachuting is avoided when:

1 − r > (h0/A0) · sin(θ/2)

This is a real trap. With h0/A0 = 5 and r = 0.9, θ must be below 2.3°, which limits the feedback frequency to about 5% of fB. A larger A0 relaxes the condition but presses the tip harder into the sample. A conventional PID therefore cannot image fragile samples quickly without either parachuting or strong tip loading. The solution is the dynamic PID controller, which adjusts its gains automatically during imaging, in particular on downhill regions (details in Section 4.6 of the book).

Questions

How does cantilever stiffness depend on its dimensions?

kc = E w d³/(4L³): proportional to width and the cube of thickness, and inversely proportional to the cube of length.

Why are short, thin cantilevers preferred for fast imaging of biological samples?

The resonance rises with d/L², so they are fast, and stiffness can still be kept low by making them thin. They respond quickly without pushing hard on the sample.

What is the effective mass in the first mode, and why do higher modes not suit biology?

About 0.24 of the beam's mass. In higher modes the effective spring constant grows as βn⁴ (about 39 times larger for n = 2), which is too stiff for fragile samples.

What is the feedback bandwidth?

The frequency at which the Z-scanner lags the sample height by π/4. It is roughly 1/(8τ), where τ is the total loop delay.

Name three ways to image faster without damaging the sample.

Reduce the scan range or number of lines, align filaments along the fast scan axis or raise protein density to lower step heights, and use a dynamic PID controller (also a faster feedback bandwidth).

What is tip parachuting, and what does it look like in an image?

The tip completely loses contact on a downhill region and takes a long time to land again. It appears as bright lines along the fast-scan direction with no topographic information.

Why can't a conventional PID image fragile samples at high speed?

Avoiding parachuting needs a small phase delay, which limits the feedback frequency, or a large free amplitude, which presses harder on the sample. A dynamic PID adjusts its gains during imaging to avoid this trade-off.
